notes: Scope: SAME (PSI-102), SAME-R (PSI-101), DAFT and DAFT-2 (PSI-47, one PSI record for both). A fifth record, PSI-115, is included because it is the PSI modelling investigation built on SAME data; its findings are simulation results (evidence_level "model or analysis").

Main sources are the final reports stored in PSI itself (Reports folders of PSI-102, PSI-101, PSI-47 and PSI-115), downloaded through the PSI web service and saved under raw/pdf as PSI-<n>_<name>.pdf with pdftotext output. They are cited with source.kind "pdf"; source.url is the PSI download URL (file id from raw/psi/files/PSI-<n>.json).
raw/pdf/PSI-47_DAFT_FactSheet.txt is pdftotext output without -layout (the two-column sheet interleaves columns with -layout); the other raw/pdf/PSI-*.txt files use -layout.

DAFT-2: no findings are filed under DAFT-2. PSI-47 is one record titled "DAFT / DAFT-2" with a single objective, and the saved sources use "DAFT-2" only as the name of the hardware kit that held the DustTrak (kits DAFT-1 to DAFT-4). All DAFT results, including the DustTrak readings, are under investigation "DAFT".

No combustion and no oxygen or pressure variation in this family: SAME and SAME-R heat samples below the ignition point in ISS cabin air inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox; DAFT burns nothing. o2_percent and pressure are null because the sources do not state them. The family therefore has no flammability-limit, flame-spread or suppression findings.

Sources disagree, recorded as found: (1) SAME-R zero-flow effect: the body of the final report says the diameter of average mass is 30% to 40% larger at zero flow, the conclusions of the same report say particles were 2 to 3 times larger than at 8 cm/s (findings on both). (2) Low gravity versus normal gravity: first SAME results say typically 50% larger count mean diameter, the SAME-R paper says typically twice the size; a 2016 review says gravity was not the dominant cause of size variation. (3) SAME air flow: final report says the system was designed for 2 to 8 cm/s, the PSI experimental table lists 5 and 10 cm/s. (4) SAME-R date: reports and NTRS say July to September 2010 (Expedition 24); the NASA feature "Smoke Particles Are Not All the SAME" says the second run was in 2011. (5) SAME-R TEM samples: the final report gives both 70 and 72. (6) SAME aging time range: 10 to 1800 s (SAME report), 11 to 1800 s (NTRS 20130000422), 11 to 800 s (NTRS 20140006585).

Some characters are lost in the PDF text: in raw/pdf/PSI-102_SAME_Final_Science_Report.txt several "µ" are a private-use glyph or missing, so quotes there stop before the unit or keep the glyph; superscripts are flattened (mg/m3, cm3). Claims give the unit as the surrounding text makes clear (micrometer).

SAME Table 1 (finding with the eight table rows): the report text says the table holds baseline runs (no aging) and 720 second aging runs; the three diameter columns are geometric mean, arithmetic mean and diameter of average mass in nm, the last column the geometric standard deviation.

Findings sourced from NTRS 20170000248 (Fire Detection Tradeoffs) and NTRS 20205008167 (2020 overview slides) are filed under SAME because they interpret SAME results; they are later NASA analyses and summaries, not SAME flight measurements (see evidence_level).
Table quotes (DETECTION findings with rows of numbers) are the table rows as pdftotext prints them, whitespace collapsed; column meaning is given in the claim from the table header in the same file.

Detector-response numbers per material from the journal paper "Evaluation of spacecraft smoke detector performance in the low-gravity environment" (Fire Safety Journal 2018, listed in PSI-101 and PSI-102) are not included: NTRS search returned no record for it and the paper is not a NASA-hosted text in this project.

source.year: for the two nasa.gov fact sheet PDFs (ids same, daft) it is the upload year in the URL (2025), the text itself is older; for the DAFT 30 Day Report (2006) and the PSI DAFT fact sheet (2005) it is the latest date named in the text, since neither carries a print date; for PSI records it is the PSI public release year.
Not fetched: PSI presentations (.ppt/.pptx) and the DAFT final and 1-year reports (.doc), which pdftotext cannot read.

Verification (2026-11-14): every finding passed tools/quotecheck.py with --refetch (82 of 82) before review. One finding was rejected (DETECTION-016) and 41 were narrowed (claim, topic, conditions, evidence_level or decision_hint); see evidence/detection.rejects.md. Each surviving finding carries a "verified" note.

Live re-download check: NTRS 20170000248 full-text PDF and the nasa.gov DAFT fact sheet PDF were downloaded again and are byte-identical (sha256) to the cached PDFs; the nasa.gov post wp-json/wp/v2/migration/309159 was downloaded again and contains the quoted sentence; the five NTRS abstracts were confirmed live by quotecheck --refetch. psi.nasa.gov could not be re-checked: the PSI web service answered HTTP 504 (PDF downloads for PSI-102 and PSI-47) and 500 (PSI-102 record) on 3 tries each, so the PSI-hosted PDFs were checked only against their cached copies (each cached .txt equals pdftotext of the cached PDF, and file ids and byte sizes match raw/psi/files/PSI-<n>.json).
DETECTION-009 keeps the report's sentence that the CMD of silicone smoke is 189 nm although Table 1 of the same report lists 189 nm as the geometric mean (arithmetic mean 257 nm); the claim says so.

investigations.name: SAME
investigations.platform: International Space Station (ISS), Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
investigations.hardware: PSI lists "Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware" (PSI spelling). The SAME apparatus: smoke generation duct with a six-sample carousel, an aging chamber with a moving piston, a diagnostics duct with three moment instruments plus a Space Shuttle and an ISS smoke detector, and a thermal precipitator.
investigations.years: Flight tests in September and early October 2007 (ISS Expedition 15). PSI investigation dates: 03-02-2001 to 02-28-2008.
investigations.pi: David L. Urban, NASA Glenn Research Center
investigations.objectives: Quantify the size of smoke particulate produced in low gravity by overheated spacecraft materials, relate the size distribution to the smoke generation and transport conditions, and give design data for future spacecraft smoke detectors.
fuels: dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) on a cotton wick (reference material)
investigations.sample_geometry: A steel heating wire wrapped around an approximately 3 mm diameter cylinder of the sample material; samples are heated below ignition (no flame). Six pre-weighed samples per carousel, 30 samples in total.

conditions.flow: System designed for air flow of 2 to 8 cm/s past the sample (final report); the PSI experimental table lists air flow of 5 and 10 cm/s.

investigations.variables: Changed between tests: sample material, air flow rate, pyrolysis (sample) temperature, and smoke aging duration (10 s to 1800 s in the aging chamber). Kept the same: heating method, about 60 s heating time, hardware and instruments.
measurements: Zeroth moment (particle number concentration): P-Trak condensation nuclei counter
First moment (diameter concentration): ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector
Third moment (mass concentration): two DustTrak light-scattering instruments, one with a 1 micrometer impactor and one with a 10 micrometer impactor
Response of a Space Shuttle (ionization) and an ISS (light scattering) smoke detector in the diagnostics duct
Smoke particles collected by a thermal precipitator on TEM grids for post-flight microscopy

findings.topic: what a spacecraft detector must look for
findings.claim: On a spacecraft the fire detection system has to target the early phase of a fire, so the primary thing to detect is pyrolysis products, not soot.
findings.quote: Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.

source.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

findings.earth_instinct: Smoke means soot from a visible flame, so a detector tuned for flaming-fire smoke is enough.

verified.support: Quote states that on a spacecraft the detection target is the early phase, so the primary target is pyrolysis products and not soot.

findings.claim: The Shuttle detector used a pump and a particle separator that rejected particulate larger than 1 micrometer; its design assumed incipient fires show up as particulate in the 0.4 to 0.7 micrometer range.
findings.quote: based their design on data that suggested incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 μm to 0.7 μm range.8 The use of a pump provided the opportunity to use a particle separator that rejected particulate larger than 1μm.

findings.quote: The small diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system, suggesting that detection of these particles against the background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution.

findings.claim: In a smoke aging run for silicone rubber the overall number count dropped substantially while the mass concentrations stayed relatively steady, consistent with particle coagulation with limited wall loss.

The first sampling interval is between 5200 and 5250 seconds and the post aging sampling interval is between 6000 and 6050 seconds. Consistent with particle coagulation with limited wall loss, the overall number count (Ptrak) decreases substantially while the mass concentrations (DustTraks) remain relatively steady.

findings.topic: three mechanisms behind larger microgravity smoke
